identity.title: World-In-World: World Models in a Closed-Loop World

problem.claim: Whether generative world models can provide embodied agents with predictive perception that improves decision making.

gap.claim: Existing evaluation is fragmented and mostly open-loop, emphasizing visual quality while leaving embodied utility unresolved.

contributions.claim: Introduces World-In-World, an open closed-loop platform for benchmarking world models in agent-environment interactions.
Provides unified online planning and a standardized action API for heterogeneous world models, with four closed-loop environments and task success as the primary metric.
Reports a data scaling law for embodied world models and identifies relationships among controllability, post-training data, inference-time compute, and closed-loop performance.

stated_novelty.claim: The authors describe World-In-World as the first open platform for closed-loop world-model benchmarking and report the first data scaling law for world models in embodied settings.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The study reports that visual quality alone does not guarantee task success, and that controllability matters more.
The study reports that scaling post-training with action-observation data is more effective than upgrading pretrained video generators.
The study reports that allocating more inference-time compute substantially improves closed-loop performance.

narrative_sequence.summary: Visual realism in generative world models motivates testing their usefulness for embodied decision making.
Open-loop, visual-quality-focused benchmarks do not resolve whether world models help agents succeed at embodied tasks.
World-In-World addresses this gap with closed-loop environments, online planning, and a standardized action interface.
The study reports controllability, action-observation post-training, and inference-time compute as key factors in closed-loop outcomes.
The authors frame closed-loop outcomes as the basis for systematic world-model assessment.

source_observation.claim: The abstract explicitly separates visual quality from task success and makes task success the primary evaluation metric.

lessons.interpretation: When a model is intended for interaction, evaluation aligned with the downstream closed-loop objective can reveal limitations hidden by component-level quality metrics.
lessons.application: Define the agent-environment success measure first, then use visual or intermediate metrics as supporting diagnostics.
lessons.exception: This is unsuitable when the research question is specifically limited to perceptual fidelity or open-loop generation quality.

source_observation.claim: The reported comparisons distinguish upgrading pretrained generators from scaling post-training with action-observation data, and identify inference-time compute as another performance lever.

lessons.interpretation: A useful abstract can make intervention dimensions explicit rather than treating model improvement as a single undifferentiated axis.
lessons.application: When presenting an empirical study, separate pretraining, interaction-data post-training, and inference-time compute as distinct experimental factors.
lessons.exception: The decomposition may be inappropriate when the study cannot vary these factors independently.

unknowns: The abstract gives no quantitative results, environment descriptions, model list, or evaluation protocol details.
The reported comparisons do not specify their baselines, compute budgets, statistical uncertainty, or conditions of applicability.
